title: Act III, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: At dusk a mysterious Third Murderer joins the first two. Banquo and Fleance approach on foot from the palace gate with a torch. The murderers attack and kill Banquo, who cries to Fleance to fly and avenge him. The light is struck out and Fleance escapes. The murderers go to report how much is done.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act III, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act III, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act III, Scene III develops the idea of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene III suggests about Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's setting and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses setting in Act III, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene III and its treatment of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's setting and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
